children.translated_text: One should construct a rasaśālā (alchemical laboratory) free from every disturbance,
in a charming region full of all medicinal herbs and furnished with a well.
In a splendid quarter belonging to the lord of yakṣas and to the thousand-eyed one,
it should be supplied with many kinds of equipment and made beautiful with an enclosure.
In the eastern quarter of the hall one should install <s>Rasabhairava</s>;
fire operations should be in the southeast, and stone work in the south.
Operations with blades should be in the southwest, washing and the like in the west;
drying should be in the northwestern corner, and piercing operations likewise in the north.
The placing of perfected substances should be done in the northeastern corner;
the collection of materials should be made for the sake of accomplishing rasa practice.
One should gather a fine sattva-extraction furnace and a splendid melting furnace,
an earthen furnace, a movable furnace, and many water troughs,
a pair of bellows, likewise tubes of bamboo and iron,
vessels made of gold, iron, bell-metal, copper, stone, and also leather,
and all the various instruments as well.
There should be churners, grinding stones, mortars, trough-shaped and round vessels,
iron and heated mortars, and pestles of the same kind,
furnished with thousands of very small holes for the purpose of sifting substances.

children.text: cālanī ca kaṭatrāṇī śilā laulī ca kaṇḍanī
children.translated_text: There should be a sieve, protective covers, a stone slab, a shaking vessel, and a pounder,
crucible clay, husks, cotton, forest dung-cakes, and prepared cakes.
There are three kinds of medicines, made respectively from minerals, living substances, and roots;

children.text: śikhitrā govaraṃ caiva śarkarā ca sitopalā ||
children.translated_text: also śikhitrā fuel, cow dung, gravel, and white stone.
There should be glass, iron, earthen, and cowrie vessels, flasks and cups,
winnowing baskets and other bamboo containers, small quick-use conches,
razors, likewise bowls, and whatever else is used there,
small bowls, karṇikā vessels, and knives for cutting vegetables.
Whatever final work is involved in sweeping the hall and cooking rasa,
and whatever else is useful there, all that, by means of the higher science,
one should collect after consecrating everything with the auspicious <s>Rasāṅkuśa</s> mantra.
Otherwise <s>Bhairava</s> takes away the energy that has entered it.

children.text: cālinī trividhā proktā tatsvarūpaṃ ca kathyate
children.translated_text: The sieve is said to be of three kinds, and its form is now explained.
Made from bamboo splints and tied together with cords,

children.text: kīrtitā sā sadā sthūladravyāṇāṃ gālane hitā
children.translated_text: that one is declared always useful for filtering coarse substances.
For the sake of sifting powders there is another sieve too, made of bamboo,
or made from the bark of karṇikāra, śālmalī, or pārijāta,
properly fashioned with a breadth of four finger-widths and considered good.
Another sieve has a span-wide coil, is wrapped in goat skin,
and has its bottom bound with horsehair cloth.
With that one should sift in order to obtain extremely fine dust.
Śikhitrā are the embers left by fire; they are regarded as kokilā charcoal.
Those embers are called kokilā when they have gone out without water.
Piṣṭaka, chagaṇa, chāṇa, upala, and utpala
and karaṇḍopalasārī are names for thoroughly dried cow-dung cakes.

children.text: kūpikā champikā siddhā golā caiva karaṇḍikā ||
children.translated_text: Kūpikā, campikā, siddhā, golā, and karaṇḍikā,

children.text: caṣakā ca kaṭorī ca vāṭikā ghoṭikā tathā
children.translated_text: and caṣakā, kaṭorī, vāṭikā, and ghoṭikā,
as well as kacolī and grāhikā are names with one and the same meaning.
Physicians versed in the rasa-saṃhitās, those who know the nighaṇṭus, and practical experts,
who know the languages of all regions, should also be gathered by practitioners.
A righteous man, truthful in speech, learned, a worshiper of <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Keśava</s>,
compassionate and lotus-handed, should be engaged in rasa medicine.
One whose hand bears marks of a banner, water pot, lotus, fish, and bow,
and whose own mark lies below the ring finger, is one whose hand possesses nectar.
A physician without proper instruction, devoid of compassion, greedy, and lacking practical reasoning,
whose hand bears black lines and is burnt-handed, should be avoided.
At the completion of cooking rasa one should always recite the Sadāghora mantra.
Assistants should be energetic, pure, brave, and strong.
Those who know mantras for confronting spirits should be employed in accomplishing treasures.
Those who are strong, vigorous, red-eyed, and dark-bodied,
and who know the science of terrifying spirits, should be employed in carrying out bali offerings.
Those who are free from greed, truthful speakers, and worshipers of gods and brahmins,
restrained and eating wholesome food, should be assigned to rasāyana work.
Those who are wealthy, generous, and furnished with all equipment,
and always devoted to the teacher's word, are suitable for discussions of metals.
Those who know the names of the various medicines, who are pure and free from deception,
and who know the languages of many regions are considered fit for gathering medicines.
For those who are pure, truthful in speech, faithful, and resolute,
whose minds are free from doubt, rasa succeeds, and not otherwise.
When rasa has been perfected through the eighteen operations, such a man is the best practitioner.
Saying, 'This is the great rasa,' he should use that rasa elsewhere.

children.text: rasasiddho bhavenmartyo dātā bhoktā na yācakaḥ
children.translated_text: A mortal perfected in rasa becomes a giver and enjoyer, not a beggar;
free from old age, honored by the world, divinely radiant, and always happy.
For the awakening of inexperienced physicians, this is taught by <s>Somadeva</s>:
the terminology of rasendra, as spoken by the treatises and by the perfected adepts.

children.text: ardhaṃ siddharasasya tailaghṛtayorlehasya bhāgo'ṣṭamaḥ saṃsiddhākhilalohacūrṇavaṭakādīnāṃ tathā saptamaḥ
children.translated_text: Half of perfected rasa, one eighth part of oil, ghee, or electuary, and likewise one seventh of pills and the like made from powders of all perfected metals,

children.text: yo dīyeta bhiṣagvarāya gadibhirnirdiśya dhanvantariṃ sarvārogyasukhāptaye nigadito bhāgaḥ sa dhānvantaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: whatever is given by patients to the best physician, after invoking <s>Dhanvantari</s>, for the attainment of complete health and happiness, is declared to be the dhānvantara share.
And the share from substances bought for medicine is indeed the eleventh part.

children.text: vaṇigbhyo gṛhyate vaidyai rudrabhāgaḥ sa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: The portion taken by physicians from merchants is called the <s>Rudrabhāga</s>, the share of Rudra.
A physician with a greedy mind who, after taking more than the proper Rudra-share,
causes an unsuitable medicine to be administered, is a betrayer of trust.
In the śāstras purification is prescribed even for those who have committed the killing of a Brahmin;
but for men who betray trust there is no purification apart from death.
Mercury, triturated dry with metals and with sulfur and the like,
when very smooth and resembling lampblack, is called <s>kajjalī</s>.

children.text: sadravā marditā saiva rasapaṅka iti smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That same substance, when triturated with liquids, is remembered as <s>rasapaṅka</s>, mercury-mud.
From mercury in a measure equal to an arka-portion, and from sulfur equal to half a niṣka, added bit by bit in the mortar,

children.text: arkātape tīvratare sagharme piṣṭī bhavetsā navanītarūpā ||
children.translated_text: under the fierce heat of the sun on a hot day, the <s>piṣṭī</s> paste becomes butter-like in form.

children.text: khalve vimardya gandhena dugdhena saha pāradam
children.translated_text: Having triturated mercury in a mortar with sulfur and milk,

children.text: peṣaṇāt piṣṭatāṃ yāti sāpi piṣṭī matā paraiḥ ||
children.translated_text: through grinding it reaches the state of a paste; that too is considered <s>piṣṭī</s> by others.
A paste made with mercury and one fourth part of gold
is a <s>pātana-piṣṭī</s>; it gives the highest success for mercury.
Silver or gold, struck down by mercury, sulfur, and the like,

children.text: samutthitaṃ hi bahuśaḥ sā kṛṣṭī hematārayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: and repeatedly brought back up, is the <s>kṛṣṭī</s> of gold and silver.

children.text: kṛṣṭī kṣiptā suvarṇāntarna varṇo hīyate tayā
children.translated_text: When <s>kṛṣṭī</s> is cast into gold, the color is not diminished by it;
the seed made with gold-kṛṣṭī is a coloring agent for mercury.
Copper joined with <s>tīkṣṇa</s> metal, melted, and repeatedly cast
into lakuca juice containing sulfur comes out as an excellent metal.
Gold reddened by that is called <s>svarṇaraktī</s>, gold-redness.
When it is cast into molten gold, it produces an intensification of color;
it is also a coloring agent for silver and produces the color of the seed.
In just this way a charming <s>tāraraktī</s>, silver-redness, should be prepared;
it is indeed a coloring agent for silver, and also a coloring agent for the seeds.

children.text: mṛtena vā baddharasena vānyallohena vā sādhitamanyaloham
children.translated_text: Another metal prepared with dead mercury, or with bound mercury, or with another metal,
when it has attained whiteness or yellowness, is the sheet called <s>dala</s>, well known for the moon and fire metals.
A metal joined with mercury that has been bound by the ābhāsa process,

children.text: sādhitaṃ cānyalohena sitaṃ pītaṃ hi taddalam ||
children.translated_text: and prepared with another metal, becomes that white or yellow <s>dala</s>.
Magnetite iron killed with <s>tāpya</s> and brought up seven times,
and lead struck down with <s>śilā</s>, again and again brought back up,

children.text: tad dvayaṃ dvipalaṃ cātha tāpyabhasma paladvayam
children.translated_text: these two, two palas in weight, and then two palas of ash of <s>tāpya</s>,

children.text: sarvaṃ nikṣipya mūṣāyāṃ saptavāraṃ dhamed dṛḍham ||
children.translated_text: should all be put into a crucible and blown strongly seven times.
That is called <s>ayo-nāga</s>; it is effective for both the body and metals.
When its pill has been made with mercury in a <s>sāraṇāyantra</s>,
and held in the mouth, it utterly destroys the whole complex of urinary disorders.
It also produces firmness of the teeth and eyesight like that of a vulture,
as well as other eye-born diseases and diseases arising above the collarbone.
Copper killed with <s>mākṣika</s> and brought up ten times,
and in the same way thoroughly purified lead: that pair amounts to four palas.
Again, killed with blue collyrium and brought up seven times,
this, when fully perfected, is called <s>śulba-nāga</s>.
The lordly mercury processed by that, when held in the mouths of men,
within only a month utterly destroys the whole complex of urinary disorders.
Within a year, for one who eats wholesome food, it removes grey hair together with wrinkles;
he becomes vulture-sighted, shining with nourishment, and endowed with complete health.

children.text: lohaṃ lohāntare kṣiptaṃ dhmātaṃ nirvāpitaṃ drave
children.translated_text: A metal cast into another metal, blown and quenched in a liquid,
when it has become pale-yellow in appearance, is called <s>piñjarī</s>.

children.text: bhāgāḥ ṣoḍaśa tārasya tathā dvādaśa bhāskaraḥ
children.translated_text: Sixteen parts of silver and likewise twelve parts of <s>bhāskara</s> metal
are melted together; by that combination it is called <s>candrārka</s>.
If another metal is inserted into the metal to be perfected through a crooked tube,
the quenching that physicians describe is indeed <s>nirvāhaṇa</s>.
The substance to be introduced in <s>nirvāhaṇa</s> should be cast in equal measure into what is to receive it;

children.text: āvāpyaṃ vāpanīye ca bhāge diṣṭe ca diṣṭavat ||
children.translated_text: and what is to be deposited should be deposited into the part specified, precisely as specified.

children.text: mṛtaṃ tarati tattoye lohaṃ vāritaraṃ hi tat ||
children.translated_text: When a dead metal floats on water, that metal is called <s>vāritara</s>, water-floating.
When rubbed between the thumb and forefinger, if it enters between their lines,
that dead metal is designated by the name <s>rekhāpūrṇa</s>, line-filling.
When combined with jaggery, guñjā, <s>sukhasparśa</s>, honey, and ghee,
it does not return to its original nature through blowing; it is called <s>apunarbhava</s>, non-reverting.

children.text: rūpyeṇa saha saṃyuktaṃ dhmātaṃ rūpyeṇa no laget
children.translated_text: When combined with silver and blown, if it does not adhere to the silver,
then that metal is called <s>niruttha</s>; it is <s>apunarbhava</s>.

children.text: evaṃ rūpyaṃ sanāgaṃ ced dhmātaṃ tāmre lagenna hi
children.translated_text: Likewise, if silver together with lead, when blown, does not adhere to copper,

children.text: tadā nirutthaṃ mantavyaṃ rañjanaṃ ca bhiṣagvaraiḥ ||
children.translated_text: then it is to be regarded by the best physicians as <s>niruttha</s> and as a coloring agent.
When, through a particular mode of <s>nirvāhaṇa</s>, each respective color comes about,
and the substance is soft and richly processed, that is called <s>bīja</s>, the seed.
This very thing is specified by physicians as <s>uttaraṇa</s>, extraction or raising,
the destruction of one metal out of two metals that have been mixed together.
By intense blowing through a crooked tube, that beating or striking is explained.

children.text: cūrṇābhraṃ śālisaṃyuktaṃ vastre baddhaṃ tu kāñjike
children.translated_text: Powdered mica, mixed with rice and tied in a cloth in sour gruel,
when it comes out through the cloth by rubbing, is called <s>dhānyābhra</s>, grain-mica.
When ore is blown in an ore-furnace together with alkaline, acidic, and solvent substances,
the essence that comes out from it is called <s>sattva</s>.
A furnace, filled to the top with coals through the act of blowing,
with them reaching the neck of the crucible, is regarded as <s>ekakoliśikhā</s>.
<s>Śikhitrā</s> are the leavings of fire; spent embers are also called <s>kokilā</s>.
<s>Kṛṣṇāṅga</s> and <s>koliśa</s> are mutually synonymous terms.

children.text: drāvaṇe sattvapāte ca mādhukāḥ khādirāḥ śubhāḥ
children.translated_text: For melting and for causing the essence to fall, madhūka and khadira woods are auspicious.

children.text: uddrāve vaṃśajāste tu svedane bādarāḥ śubhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But for the upward melting, bamboo-derived fuels are used; for steaming, badara wood is suitable.
From the apparatus called <s>Vidyādhara</s>, when it has been triturated with ginger juice,
the mercury that has been drawn out is called hiṅgula-drawn mercury.
Bronze mixed with a little tāla, struck through a bent tube,
becomes that copper freed from tin; it is described as ghoṣa-drawn.
Twenty palas of purified nāga, made into small discs,
should be smeared with śilā ground together with rūpikā milk.
After enclosing it in a sealed pair of earthen saucers, one should cook it with a kroḍa-puṭa.
One should carefully cook it again and again until it becomes ash.
Having thoroughly triturated it with jaggery, guggulu, guñjā, ghee, and sāragha,
then, after confining it inside a crucible, it is again raised up by blowing.
Having again performed the cakrānta procedure with mercury measured by the pala,
one should smear it with the milk of white arka and also with śilā.
One should cook this with gaja-puṭa heatings for twenty turns,

children.text: puṭe puṭe hi nāgasya kuryādutthānaṃ khalu ||
children.translated_text: and at each heating one should indeed bring about the raising of the nāga.
One should quench it properly ten times with liquids of nīlajyotis.
Thus prepared, the lead is then reduced to only a karṣa in amount.
It is called secret nāga and is said to be the best <s>rasa-rasāyana</s>.

children.text: niṣkamātre tu nāge 'smin lohakhāryāṃ drute sati ||
children.translated_text: When a niṣka measure of this nāga has melted in an iron cauldron,

children.text: svato lakṣaguṇāṃ haimīṃ śalākāṃ grasati dhruvam
children.translated_text: it certainly swallows of itself a golden rod a hundred-thousandfold greater.
Heated in kusumbha oil, it certainly emits that gold.
This secret path has been taught; <s>Svacchandabhairava</s> declares it.

children.text: tīkṣṇaṃ nīlāñjanopetaṃ dhmātaṃ hi bahuśo dṛḍham ||
children.translated_text: Tīkṣṇa metal mixed with blue collyrium, blown firmly many times,
soft, black, and quickly melting, is called excellent nāga.
The re-arising of what has been killed is what is described by the name utthāpana.
The insertion of a melted substance into a liquid is regarded as ḍhālana.
Thirty palas of nāga, triturated with bhānu milk,
should be rubbed and heated until only a karṣa remains.
It never undergoes loss, even through a thousand puṭa heatings.
This capala, born from nāga, has been described by the theorists.

children.text: itthaṃ ca capalaḥ kāryo vaṅgasyāpi na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this same way capala should also be prepared from vaṅga; there is no doubt.
Mercury, merely touched by a hand that has touched it, becomes bound.

children.text: sa raso dhātuvādeṣu śasyate na rasāyane ||
children.translated_text: That mercury is praised in metallic operations, but not in rasāyana.
This was proclaimed by <s>Lokanātha</s>, who is called <s>Kharpaṇa</s>.
Fine powder of bhrāmaka stone, combined with one-fifth part mercury,
should be triturated with water from the root of kumārī for one day.
And also with fresh juice of cāṅgerī, without interruption for one day.
In this way one should triturate it for three days with water washed through bhūnāga.
Then, with one pala of nāga and with the same amount of trapu,
and with ten niṣkas of rasendra, one should make a smooth paste.
After combining it with the paste, one should triturate it as before.
Then, with essential rasendra and with the essence of rasaka,

children.text: piṣṭīṃ kṛtvā tu pūrveṇa pūrvakalkena yojayet ||
children.translated_text: having made a paste, one should combine it with the earlier paste.
After kindling the fire, one should dry it with warm sour gruel.
With half a pala of purified sasyaka and with the juice of roasted guñjā,
having triturated it with sour gruels, one should make pills the size of peppercorns.
Having sealed them in a vajra crucible and made the sealing of the joint,
one should blow it properly with nine śikhitra fuels and with two bellows.
Then, taking up on all sides the essence that has entered the crucible,
one should blow it in an open crucible with a bent tube for purification.

children.text: daśaśāṇaṃ hi tatsattvaṃ bhasmanā lavaṇena ca ||
children.translated_text: Ten śāṇas of that essence, together with ash and salt,
should be wrapped with sour gruel and dried by means of a puṭa heating.
When two niṣkas of it are present, with the ash previously described,
one should blow eighty times as much nāga and drive it out.
By this amount that previously prepared mercury is not digested in any way.
This capala has been described by <s>Śambhu</s>, lord of the world.

children.text: anenāpi rasaḥ śīghraṃ badhyate pūrvavat sukham ||
children.translated_text: By this also mercury is quickly and easily bound, just as before.
When it has been heated ten times with powders of kāravallī root,
it becomes freed from nāga and takes in the entire morsel.
The mouth in an open crucible becomes exceedingly superior.
This mercury, whose morsel has been digested, becomes able to produce body and metal.
This has been stated with complete certainty by the illustrious <s>Somadeva</s>.
Washed with waters containing the dung of bhūbhujaṅga, the powder is removed;
that black-colored substance is called dhauta by the teachers of rasa.
The joining of two substances by blowing is called dvandvana.
The casting of a portion into silver and the like, in lower-colored gold,
or the decrease of color by leaves, is considered by the practitioners to be bhañjinī.
The silverness or goldness in iron that arises from pataṅgī paste,

children.text: dināni katicit sthitvā yātyasau palikā matā
children.translated_text: after remaining for some days, passes away; that is regarded as palikā.
And what, having been colored by mercury or by metal, after blowing or after a long time,
comes out, that is specified by the name pataṅgī-rāga.

children.text: drute dravyāntare kṣepo lohādyaiḥ kriyate hi yaḥ
children.translated_text: The insertion into another molten substance, which is done with metals and the like,

children.text: sa āvāpaḥ pratīvāpaḥ sa evācchādanaṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: is āvāpa and pratīvāpa; that same is regarded as ācchādana.
When iron is molten and standing in the fire, after waiting eight nimeṣas,
the sprinkling on of water is called abhiṣeka.

children.text: taptasyāpsu vinikṣepo nirvāpaḥ snapanaṃ ca tat
children.translated_text: The plunging of something heated into water is nirvāpa, and that is also snapana.
A <s>pratīvāpa</s> operation should be performed in molten metal that is very pure.
When the fire has blazing flames and is accompanied by a white upward rising,
then it should be known as a pure <s>āvarta</s>; that is the time for the extraction of the essence.
When, during blowing, a flame resembling the substance to be melted is seen,
this is its readiness for melting; it is called <s>bījāvarta</s>.
What is cold even while standing in the fire is said to be <s>svāṅgaśītala</s>, cold in its own body;
and what has coldness drawn from the fire is called <s>bahiḥśītala</s>, cold externally.
The cooking of something placed in a swing apparatus with alkalis, acids, or medicines
is called <s>svedana</s>, and it causes impurities to become loosened.
Grinding together with the prescribed medicines, with all acids and also with sour gruel,
is called <s>mardana</s>, and it destroys external impurity.
That which, through the medicines prescribed for grinding, makes the substance lose its ground-paste condition
is indeed <s>mūrchana</s>; it destroys the coating from tin and related base-metal contact.
The bringing about of paste-like condition through the destruction of its own form:
mercury subdued by the learned in this way is called <s>naṣṭapiṣṭa</s>.
The restoring of its own form through the application of steaming, sunlight, and the like
is called <s>utthāpana</s>; it removes the mishap of mūrchana.
The extraction, upward, downward, and sideways, from an apparatus, of mercury ground with the stated medicines
is called by the name <s>pātana</s>; it destroys the coating born from contact with tin and nāga metal.
The keeping of mercury mixed with water and rock salt for three days
in an <s>āsthāpanī</s> jar is called <s>rodhana</s>.
For mercury that has gained potency through rodhana, in order to stop its mobility,

children.text: kriyate yo ghaṭe svedaḥ proktaṃ niyamanaṃ hi tat ||
children.translated_text: the sweating that is performed in a pot is called <s>niyamana</s>.
When mercury is combined with metals, minerals, roots, and the like and placed inside a pot,

children.text: grāsārthaṃ tridinaṃ svedo dīpanaṃ tanmataṃ budhaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: the three-day sweating for the sake of taking a morsel is considered by the wise to be <s>dīpana</s>.
The measure consisting of morsel-substances for this much mercury,
when it is stated as 'so much,' is called the <s>grāsamāna</s>, the measure of the morsel.

children.text: grāsasya cāraṇaṃ garbhe drāvaṇaṃ jāraṇaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: The conveying of the morsel, the melting in the womb, and the digestion of it
are the three forms of <s>jāraṇā</s> taught by the best experts.

children.text: grāsaḥ piṇḍaḥ parīṇāmaḥ tisraścākhyāḥ parāḥ smṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Grāsa</s>, <s>piṇḍa</s>, and <s>parīṇāma</s> are remembered as its three further names;

children.text: samukhā nirmukhā ceti jāraṇā dvividhā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and jāraṇā is again of two kinds, with a mouth and without a mouth.
Mouthless <s>jāraṇā</s> is said to occur through the taking in of seed in portions.

children.text: śuddhaṃ svarṇaṃ ca rūpyaṃ ca bījamityabhidhīyate ||
children.translated_text: Pure gold and silver are called the <s>bīja</s>, the seed.
The insertion of seed to the extent of a sixty-fourth part is called the mouth.
When this has been done, mercury becomes mouth-bearing and eager for morsels.
It becomes capable of consuming even hard metals.

children.text: iyaṃ hi samukhā proktā jāraṇā mṛgacāriṇā ||
children.translated_text: This is called <s>samukhā jāraṇā</s>, according to <s>Mṛgacārin</s>.
Through conjunction with divine medicines, when it remains in exposed furnaces,
the one that consumes all metals and the rest has a demon-like mouth.
The placing of a morsel in the mouth of mercury is considered <s>cāraṇā</s>.
The melting in the belly of what has been swallowed is called internal melting.
But liquefying compact essence and the like externally
for the sake of the mercury-lord's digestion is called external melting.

children.text: nirlepatvaṃ dravatvaṃ ca tejastvaṃ laghutā tathā
children.translated_text: Non-adherence, fluidity, fiery brilliance, lightness,
and union with mercury: these five are the marks of a melted state.
When, by combination with husked grain and similar substances, metal, mineral, and the like
always remain in liquid form, that is called <s>druti</s>.
The digestion of a melted morsel through the use of a <s>viḍa</s> apparatus and the like
is called <s>jāraṇā</s>; its varieties exist by the ten million.
Alkalis, acids, sulfur and the like, urines, and likewise sharp salts,
used for the digestion of mercury's morsel, are called its <s>viḍa</s>.
The production of yellow and other colors in mercury
through the digestion of well-prepared seed-metals and the like is called <s>rañjana</s>.
The casting of gold and the like into mercury that is in an oil apparatus,
which produces greater penetration in metal, is called <s>sāraṇā</s>.
Mercury furnished with a penetrating medicine and cast into a substance

children.text: vedha ityucyate tajjñaiḥ sa cānekavidhaḥ smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: is called <s>vedha</s> by those who know it; and it is remembered as being of many kinds.
Smearing, casting, lance-contact, what is called smoke, and what is termed sound:

children.text: lepena kurute lohaṃ svarṇaṃ vā rajataṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: by smearing it makes metal into gold or silver.

children.text: lepavedhaḥ sa vijñeyaḥ puṭamatra ca saukaram
children.translated_text: That should be known as <s>lepavedha</s>; the heating process is easy in this case.

children.text: prakṣepaṇaṃ drute lohe vedhaḥ syāt kṣepasaṃjñitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Casting into molten metal is the penetration called <s>kṣepa</s>.
The taking up of a molten substance with mercury held by tongs,
which makes gold and the like, is called <s>kuntavedha</s>.
When fire is smoking, from the smoke of mercury thrown inside it,
the production of gold and the like in metal is called <s>dhūmavedha</s>.
Through the blowing of a small quantity of metal with mercury placed at the mouth,
the production of the state of gold or silver is called <s>śabdavedha</s>.
The removal of blackness and the like from a substance penetrated by mercury,
and the making manifest of its color, is called <s>udghāṭana</s>.
When, together with alkalis, acids, and medicines, it is carefully sealed in a vessel
and buried in the ground, that is called <s>svedana</s>.
When a vessel containing mercury mixed with medicines is carefully sealed
and placed inside a hearth with constant fire, that is called <s>saṃnyāsa</s>.
These two, <s>svedana</s> and <s>saṃnyāsa</s>, certainly belong to the king of rasas;
they generate qualities and powers, and they also cause rapid pervasion.

children.text: rasanigamamahābdheḥ somadevaḥ samantāt sphuṭataraparibhāṣā nāma ratnāni hṛtvā
children.translated_text: From the great ocean of the rasa scriptures, <s>Somadeva</s>, having taken on every side the jewels called very clear definitions,

children.text: vyaracayadatiyatnāttair imāṃ kaṇṭhamālāṃ kalayati bhiṣagagryo maṇḍanārthaṃ sabhāyām ||
children.translated_text: composed this necklace with great effort from them, so that the foremost physician may wear it as an ornament in an assembly.
When this chapter has been read by a rasa practitioner who has mastered the recitation,

children.text: rasakarmāṇi kurvāṇo na sa muhyati kutracit ||
children.translated_text: he, while performing rasa operations, does not become confused anywhere.
Now the instruments, the many devices of rasatantra, will be explained
briefly by <s>Somadeva</s> at present, after he has examined them.
Because mercury is restrained with effort by the best practical experts
in order to carry out operations beginning with sweating, therefore it is called a yantra (instrument).
Having wrapped medicinal mercury in birch bark and threefold cloth,

children.text: rasapoṭṭalikāṃ kāṣṭhe dṛḍhaṃ baddhvā guṇena hi ||
children.translated_text: and having firmly tied the rasa-pouch to a stick with a cord,
so that it remains moving while hanging inside a jar full of the joining liquid,
one should light the fire below according to the procedure stated for each case.
This is called the dolāyantra; that same apparatus is known as the sweating device.
The mortar-apparatus is declared to be threefold for operations such as trituration.
One is made of stone without an outlet, and another is produced from iron.
It is ten finger-widths high and, indeed, has a length measured by a kalā-like span of fingers;
it is nine finger-widths in breadth and likewise as many rasa-measured finger-widths deep.
Its neck is two finger-widths wide, very smooth, and its basin is shaped like a half-moon;
and the grinding surface is ten finger-widths: this is remembered as the apparatus called a khalva mortar.
In this, five palas of mercury should be triturated for purification.
In other mortars too one should purify it according to the suitability of each preparation.
A round khalva mortar is twelve finger-widths broad
and four finger-widths deep, made very smooth in the middle.
The pestle is flattened below and easy to grasp at its crest.
The iron khalva is nine finger-widths long and six finger-widths deep.
The pestle is eight finger-widths; this is indeed called the heated khalva.
Having made a furnace in the form of a khalva, it should be filled with charcoal.

children.text: tasyāṃ niveśitaṃ khalvaṃ pārśve bhastrikayā dhamet
children.translated_text: The khalva placed in it should be blown at the side with bellows.
The paste triturated in it, combined with alkalis and acids,
melts with great speed from the sweating; there is no doubt about this.
Made of magnetic iron, this one becomes superior by a crore-fold.
Where, in an iron vessel, there are two rings on the sides,
and a smaller vessel of the same kind has a chamber pierced by rings,
having set it upon the former vessel, one should put into the small vessel
amalgamated mercury, filling the large vessel with kāñjika sour gruel.
One should sweat it in this way for two watches for the sake of raising up the mercury.
This is the valabhīyantra, the cause of improving the quality of rasa.
In a vessel made of fine magnetic iron, the mercury becomes richer in quality.
It is properly eight finger-widths in measure, round, and flattened at the bottom,
and below the neck for four finger-widths it is furnished with a trough
four finger-widths broad and deep, firmly fastened.
The covering pot for it is sixteen finger-widths broad at the base
and is furnished with a neck nine finger-widths broad.

children.text: pūrvaghaṭyāṃ rasaṃ kṣiptvā nyubjāṃ dadyāt parāṃ ghaṭīm
children.translated_text: After putting mercury in the first pot, one should place the other pot upside down over it.
Above and below, all around, it should be furnished with a firm rim.
One should pour water into the rimmed trough and kindle fire beneath.
This is indeed the upward-distillation apparatus, as described by <s>Nandi</s>.
Into the upper and lower bowls one should place another bowl facing downward,
a small flat-bottomed bowl whose interior surface has been smeared with mercury.

children.text: kṣiptvā tāṃ paṅkile garte jvālayenmūrdhni pāvakam
children.translated_text: Having placed it in a muddy pit, one should kindle fire on its top.
That is indeed the downward-distillation apparatus; so it is described.
One should place mercury in a jar fitted with a long tube bent downward.
That tube should be inserted into the belly of another jar.
Then, after properly sealing the mouths of the two jars with clay,
one should light an intense fire beneath the mercury jar.

children.text: itarasmin ghaṭe toyaṃ prakṣipet svādu śītalam
children.translated_text: Into the other jar one should pour sweet, cold water.
This is called the oblique-distillation apparatus by the practical experts.
The threefold distillation is taught; indeed there is a triad of instruments.

children.text: pātanaiśca vinā sūto na tarāṃ doṣamujhati ||
children.translated_text: Without distillations, mercury certainly does not give up its impurity.
Why is it not freed from faults by just three upward distillations?
Because in cooking, by separation and by conjunction with another substance,
various qualities indeed arise from transferring it into another vessel.
Rice grains become freed from dirt by the mortar, pestle, and water.
Great purification is achieved by distillation alone, as described by <s>Nandi</s>.
In a vessel with a wide mouth, filled with water, one should place

children.text: kharparaṃ pṛthukaṃ samyak prasare tasya madhyame
children.translated_text: a broad potsherd properly in the middle of its spread surface.

children.text: ālavālaṃ viḍaiḥ kṛtvā tanmadhye pāradaṃ kṣipet ||
children.translated_text: Having made a basin with viḍa salts, one should put mercury in its middle.
After placing viḍa above and below and carefully covering it with a lid,
a heating by puṭa is applied according to suitability; that is stated to be
the instrument named kacchapa, and it is prescribed for the digestion of rasa.
Having made an iron crucible bearing the shape of an eggplant,
measuring a span and made from magnetic iron,
or else produced from ordinary iron, below the neck by two finger-widths,
one should make a ring two finger-widths wide around the middle region below the neck.
It should have a cover-support and a ring as broad as a tamarind leaf.
The cover should fit inside, have a crest, and have closely joined seams.

children.text: tale pravihitacchidraṃ bhāṇḍaṃ kṛtvā hy adhomukham ||
children.translated_text: Having made a vessel with a hole placed in its bottom, turned downward,

children.text: tatraināṃ lambayenmūrdhni nirudhya ca viśoṣya ca
children.translated_text: one should suspend this there at the top, seal it, and dry it.
Then one should attach the neck of the dish and apply a <s>puṭa</s> heating that produces fire.
An apparatus of this form is called the <s>antarālika</s> apparatus.
By it one should perform the liquefaction of sulfur and also internal liquefaction.

children.text: tāpīṃ mūṣāṃ mṛdā kṛtvā dṛḍhāṃ cāratnimātrikām
children.translated_text: Having made a heating crucible of clay, firm and measuring one <s>aratni</s>,
very firm in its middle region and furnished with a two-finger hole,
one should place a <s>khārī</s> made of magnetite iron above the sulfur.
One should fill the heating vessel all around with clean sand.

children.text: tāṃ ca cullyāṃ samāropya kṣepaṃ kṣepaṃ viḍadravam
children.translated_text: Having set it on the stove, and repeatedly adding liquid <s>viḍa</s>,
one should then kindle a fire whose flame is the measure of a big toe.
All substances such as iron and mica should be made to digest thoroughly into the mercury.
This is called the <s>tāpikā-yantra</s>, easy to use for the digestion of mercury.

children.text: sthālyāṃ vinikṣipya rasādi vastu svarṇādi khāryā prapidhāya bhūyaḥ
children.translated_text: Having put mercury and the other substance into a dish, and further covered it with a gold or other <s>khārī</s>,

children.text: amlena cordhve lavaṇādi vastu cullyāṃ pacettat pratigarbhayantram ||
children.translated_text: one should cook it on the stove, with sour liquid and salt or similar material above; that is the <s>pratigarbhayantra</s>.
One should very carefully seal a <s>khārī</s>, a <s>malla</s>, and an inner dish.

children.text: sthālyāṃ mṛdo'thavā khāryāṃ kṣiptvā vastu nirudhya ca ||
children.translated_text: Or, after putting the substance in a clay dish or in a <s>khārī</s> and sealing it,
and after adding sour liquid and the like and closing it, the cooking is done in the <s>garbhayantraka</s>.
A round iron cup, with an upward rod whose end is bent,
is indeed the <s>pālikā-yantra</s>, meant for the digestion of <s>bali</s>.
A vessel holding four <s>prasthas</s> of water, with an opening of four fingers,
is called the <s>ghaṭa-yantra</s>; it is regarded as useful for moistening or replenishing.

children.text: vidhāya vartulaṃ gartaṃ mallamatra nidhāya ca ||
children.translated_text: Having made a round pit, one should place a <s>malla</s> in it.
Then one should place there a good brick with a pit in its middle.
Around the pit one should make a small wall one finger high.

children.text: garte sūtaṃ vinikṣipya gartāsye vasanaṃ kṣipet
children.translated_text: Having put mercury in the pit, one should put cloth over the mouth of the pit.

children.text: nikṣipya gandhakaṃ tatra mallenāsyaṃ nirudhya ca ||
children.translated_text: Having placed sulfur there and sealed the mouth with a <s>malla</s>,
and having properly sealed the space between the <s>malla</s> and the little wall with clay,

children.text: vanopalaiḥ puṭaṃ deyaṃ kapotākhyaṃ na cādhikam ||
children.translated_text: one should give a <s>kapota</s>-type <s>puṭa</s> with forest cow-dung cakes, and no stronger one.
This is indeed the <s>iṣṭikā-yantra</s>; by it one should digest sulfur.
Having placed a dish over another dish and sealed it properly,
one should put water in the upper dish and kindle fire below.
This is the <s>vidyādhara</s> apparatus, meant for extracting from cinnabar.

children.text: yatra sthālyupari sthālīṃ nyubjāṃ dattvā nirudhya ca
children.translated_text: Where one places an inverted dish over a lower dish and seals it,
that apparatus is called the <s>ḍamaruka</s>; it is useful for making ash of mercury.
One should make a pit in the middle of a <s>malla</s>; in it are mercury together with sulfur.
Around the pit one should make a wall two fingers high.
Then one should cover it properly with a crucible shaped like a cow's udder.
Having sealed it properly with watery clay, to the same height as the pit,
one should then pour in water and kindle fire below.
This is called the <s>nābhi-yantra</s>, as taught by the all-knowing <s>Nandī</s>.
By this, mercury digests smokelessly with purified sulfur.
When it is rubbed with decoction of <s>barbūra</s> until it is like an electuary,
fine rust powder from digested metal, mixed with powdered jaggery,

children.text: iyaṃ hi jalamṛtproktā durbhedyā salilaiḥ khalu ||
children.translated_text: this is called water-clay; it is truly hard for waters to break.
With chalk, salt, and rust, rubbed with buffalo milk,
there is fire-clay, able indeed to withstand the heat of a fierce fire.

children.text: etayā mṛtsnayā ruddho na gantuṃ kṣamate rasaḥ
children.translated_text: When sealed with this clay, mercury is not able to escape,
like a man bound by the mature love of a clever woman.
<s>Nandī</s>, <s>Nāgārjuna</s>, and <s>Brahmajyotir Munīśvara</s>,
and also <s>Śrī Somadeva</s>, know this; no one else on earth does.
A crucible with another crucible inserted into its belly, evenly round at the beginning and end,

children.text: cipiṭāṃ ca tale proktaṃ grastayantraṃ manīṣibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: and said to be flattened at the bottom, is the <s>grasta-yantra</s> according to the wise.
It has been taught by knowers of mercury for the binding of the lordly mercury.
There are two crucibles shaped like eggplants; below the neck of those two, indeed,
there is a tube one span long, coated with clay and with very well joined seams.
In one of them one should put mercury, and in the other powdered sulfur.
Having sealed the mouths of the crucibles, one should place them in a sand apparatus.
One should kindle fire below; this is called the <s>tulā-yantra</s>.
It is proclaimed for the digestion of <s>śilā</s>, <s>tālaka</s>, and sulfur-stone.

children.text: sthālyāṃ tāmrādi nikṣipya mallenāsyaṃ nirudhya ca ||
children.translated_text: Having put copper or the like into a dish and sealed the mouth with a <s>malla</s>,
it is cooked while placed in the dish; this is called the <s>sthālī-yantra</s>.
Inside the belly of a large vessel one should place clean sand.
After it has been raised to the measure of a span, one should then set there
an unbaked clay furnace, twelve fingers high,
six fingers wide and made very smooth in the middle.
The cover should be five fingers across, sharp-pointed, and shaped like a crown.

children.text: na nyūnā nādhikā koṣṭhī kaṇṭhato masṛṇā bahiḥ
children.translated_text: The furnace should be neither too small nor too large, smooth outside from the neck downward.
Into the furnace one should put six palas of sulfur, finely powdered.
Then, having placed an iron tripod and fixed it firmly,

children.text: tasyāṃ ca vinyaset khārīṃ lauhīṃ vā kāntalohajām ||
children.translated_text: on it one should set a <s>khārī</s>, either iron or made of magnetite iron.
Into that one should put purified mercury, measuring twenty palas.
And one should treat the <s>sūta</s> (mercury) that has digested sulfur with the juices of garlic.
Having covered it with the previously described lid, with the point directed downward,
one should make the sealing of the joint with lime, clay, molasses, and the like.
When the joint-seal has dried, one should throw sand over it.
Then, having stopped up the mouth of the vessel, one should kindle fire beneath it.
For three watches it should be fierce; then the smoke produced from the sulfur
adheres to the lid, melts, and falls down into the <s>rasa</s> (mercurial substance).

children.text: evaṃ hi ṣaḍguṇaṃ gandhaṃ bhuktvā sūto guṇī bhavet
children.translated_text: Thus, after the <s>sūta</s> (mercury) has consumed six times its measure of sulfur, it becomes endowed with good qualities.
It produces all the special qualities prescribed in the procedure.
This furnace-apparatus has indeed been proclaimed by <s>Nandi</s>.
One should carefully place it in a vessel filled with five āḍhakas of sand.
When a mercury ball and the like are cooked in it, it is called the sand apparatus.
In the same way, from the placing of salt, it is called the salt apparatus.
Having made an iron vessel eight finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths high,

children.text: kaṇṭhādho dvyaṅgule deśe jalādhāraṃ hi tatra ca ||
children.translated_text: one should make a water receptacle there, two finger-breadths below the neck.
One should insert thin iron rods crosswise, laid across it,
and place thin gold leaves upon them.
Below the vessel one should put the fumigant that will be described hereafter.
One should cover that vessel with another vessel turned upside down.

children.text: mṛdā vilipya saṃdhiṃ ca vahniṃ prajvālayedadhaḥ
children.translated_text: After plastering the joint with clay, one should kindle the fire below.
By that, the leaves become blackened and treated according to the stated rule.
The <s>rasa</s> then moves swiftly, attaining liquefaction and internal liquefaction.
The fumigation of gold leaves with <s>kajjalyā</s>, made from sulfur, ālaka, and śilā, or with mṛtāhi,
is proclaimed to be supreme.
For silver, one should fumigate silver leaves with calcined tin.
One should also fumigate with suitable <s>rasas</s> and <s>uparasas</s> (secondary minerals).
This is called the fumigation apparatus for carrying substances used in digestion.

children.text: sthūlasthālyāṃ dravaṃ kṣiptvā vāso baddhvā mukhe dṛḍham
children.translated_text: Having put liquid into a large cooking pot and tied cloth firmly over its mouth,

children.text: tatra svedyaṃ vinikṣipya pidhānyā prapidhāya ca ||
children.translated_text: one should place there the substance to be steamed and cover it thoroughly with a lid.
One should kindle fire beneath it; that is the <s>kuṇḍaka-yantra</s> (pit apparatus).
Other wise men call this the steaming apparatus.

children.text: yadvā sthālyāṃ jalaṃ kṣiptvā tṛṇaṃ dattvā mukhopari
children.translated_text: Or, having put water in a pot and placed grass over its mouth,
one should put in the substance to be steamed and cover it thoroughly with a lid.
One should light the fire underneath; this too is the <s>kuṇḍa-yantra</s> (pit apparatus).
Into a hole below the neck of the vessel one should insert a bamboo tube.
After placing two bronze vessels as a closed capsule filled with water,

children.text: nālāsyaṃ tatra saṃyojya dṛḍhaṃ taccāpi kārayet ||
children.translated_text: one should join the mouth of the tube there and make that also firm.
The <s>rasa</s> (mercury), first placed in that jar together with the prescribed substances,

children.text: agninā tāpito nālāt toye tasmin patatyadhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: is heated by fire and falls from the tube down into that water.
So long as the whole vessel becomes at least somewhat hot,
a fixation of <s>rasa</s> occurs; this is the <s>ḍhekī-yantra</s>.

children.text: ūrdhvaṃ vahnir adhaścāpo madhye tu rasasaṃgrahaḥ
children.translated_text: Fire is above, water below, and the collection of <s>rasa</s> is in the middle.
This is called <s>somānala</s>; it digests mica and similar substances.
Mercury placed inside an iron tube, in a vessel filled with salt,
is sealed and cooked by the wise person; this is called the tube apparatus.
Now the clay called <s>mūṣā</s> (crucible), its arrangement in various shapes,
and its application according to rule are described by <s>Somadeva</s>.

children.text: mūṣā hi koṣṭhikā proktā kumudī karahārikā
children.translated_text: The <s>mūṣā</s> is called koṣṭhikā, kumudī, and karahārikā;
it is also called pātanī and vahnimitrā by the practitioners of <s>rasavāda</s> (alchemy).
Because it steals away the faults belonging to crucible-work, it is called <s>mūṣā</s>.
Its material should be clay and also metal.
Better even a single kākiṇī that has come out from the mouth of a crucible
than, for honorable people, a hundred thousand gained by bowing down to bad men; shame on it.
In fastening the crucible and its lid, the binding is the smearing of the joint.
Closing, perforating, and close adhesion together constitute the sealing of the joint.
Clay that is pale and coarse, and gravel that is reddish-white,
being able to endure prolonged heating, is highly praised for the purpose of a crucible.
In its absence, anthill clay and potter's clay are stated to be suitable.

children.text: yā mṛttikā dagdhatuṣaiḥ śaṇena śikhitrakairvā hayaladdinā ca
children.translated_text: Clay which has been mixed with burnt husks, hemp, peacock-feathers, and horse dung,

children.text: lauhena daṇḍena ca kuṭṭitā sā sādhāraṇā syātkhalu mūṣikārthe ||
children.translated_text: and pounded with an iron rod, is indeed ordinary for crucible use.
White stones, burnt husks, peacock-feathers, and hemp cloth,
dung and slag should be combined with the crucible clay as appropriate.
Three parts clay, two parts hemp and dung, and one part burnt husk, stone, and the like,
with half a part of slag: after breaking them up, one should make a vajra-crucible for the extraction of essence.
Clay arising from an anthill, furnished with burnt charcoal and husks,
combined with the respective <s>viḍa</s> salts and smeared with those respective <s>viḍa</s> salts,

children.text: tayā yā vihitā mūṣā yogamūṣeti kathyate
children.translated_text: forms a crucible made in that way, which is called a <s>yoga-mūṣā</s>.
Mercury prepared by means of it becomes still richer in qualities.
With <s>gāra</s>, washed <s>bhūnāga</s>, hemp, and burnt husks as well,
crucible clay in equal portions, kneaded with buffalo milk,
boiled for just a fortnight and turned over many times,
forms a crucible said to be capable of melting diamond.
A crucible rich in sixfold burnt <s>gāra</s>, furnished with slag, charcoal, and hemp,
and made with black clay, is called a <s>gāra-mūṣā</s>.
Even through two watches of excessive blowing, it does not melt in the fire.
Cloth, charcoal, and husks are in equal amounts, and the clay is four times as much.
Gāra, equal in amount to the clay, is also rubbed down with all these.

children.text: varamūṣeti nirdiṣṭā yāmaṃ vahniṃ saheta ca ||
children.translated_text: It is specified as the excellent crucible, and it can withstand fire for a yāma.
Mixed with dust from the red group and steeped in water of the red group,
a crucible smeared with that clay is coated with kṣitikhecara.
It is called the varṇamūṣā (coloring crucible), and it is employed for heightening color.
In the same way, with the white group, it is known as the silver crucible.
Made from clay arising from the respective viḍa and smeared with the respective viḍa,
it is called a viḍamūṣā, for operations aimed at the body and at metals.
With gāra, bhūnāga, and dhauta, with husk-ash and hemp,
in equal parts, a crucible clay is prepared, kneaded with buffalo milk.
It is boiled for only a fortnight and is described in many ways.
A crucible made from it is smeared with the blood of bedbugs.
With the roots of balā and abdadhāvanī, it is the krauñcikā for melting diamond.
When used in melting, it withstands fire for four yāmas.
Substances may come to a molten state through the application of blowing in a crucible.
The brief lifting out that is done is called the replenishing of the crucible.
In an eggplant-shaped crucible, after attaching a tube ten finger-widths long,
it should rise upward like a dhattūra flower, firm and joined like an embracing blossom.
Eight finger-widths high and perforated, this is the vṛntāka crucible.
By means of it one should draw out the sattva (metallic essence) of soft substances such as kharpara.
The crucible that has the shape of a cow's teat and a lid furnished with a crest

children.text: sattvānāṃ drāvaṇe śuddhau sā mūṣā gostanī bhavet ||
children.translated_text: is the gostanī crucible, used in the melting and purification of essences.
The mallamūṣā is defined as that made from the enclosing of two malla vessels.
It is taught for sweating parpaṭī and similar preparations of rasa.
That which has the form of a potter's vessel, firm and thoroughly baked,
is called the baked crucible and is used for cooking poṭalī and similar preparations.
Round like a ball, without a mouth, and containing the substance to be heated by puṭa,
it is called the golamūṣā, a quick container for enclosing substances.

children.text: tale yā kūrparākārā kramād upari vistṛtā
children.translated_text: That which is shaped like an elbow at the bottom and gradually spreads upward,
large like a large eggplant stalk, is regarded as the great crucible.
It is used for the puṭa heating and melting of iron, mica-essence, and the like.
The crucible that has the shape of a chest, with measured depth, length, and breadth,
six finger-widths in measure, is called the mañjūṣā crucible.
Having buried that crucible in the ground, one should then apply the puṭa heating above it.
The crucible that is flat at the base, round, and eight finger-widths high
is called the pestle-crucible; it is useful for rasa bound in a cakrī.
For the extraction of essences and for the purification of extracted essences,
there are furnaces of various shapes; their characteristics are now stated.
It is raised to the height of a royal cubit, and its length and breadth are half of that.

children.text: caturasrā ca kuḍyena veṣṭitā mṛnmayena hi ||
children.translated_text: It is square and enclosed by a wall made of clay.
In one wall one should make a pit with a span's measure of opening.

children.text: dvāraṃ sārdhavitastyā ca saṃmitaṃ sudṛḍhaṃ śubham ||
children.translated_text: The door should measure one and a half spans, firm and well made.
Below the threshold it should be arranged suitably for blowing.
The wall above the upper part should measure a prādeśa.
A door should also be made above, measuring a prādeśa.
Then, after closing it with bricks and smearing the joint of the door,
one should fill it with charcoal and blow it with two bellows.
Through the upper door one should put in charcoal and the substance to be blown.
One should also put in, again and again, five balls for extracting sattva.
This is the charcoal furnace, which extracts the essence of hard substances.
In firm ground one should make a pit, well formed and measuring a span,
round in shape; then in its middle one should prepare another pit.
It should be furnished with a breadth and depth of four finger-widths.
From the pit to the level of the ground it should have a transverse tube.
It should be somewhat raised outside and sloping down toward the pit.
Over the inner pit one should place a clay disk provided with five holes.
Having filled the furnace with charcoal, one should blow it with a single bellows.
This is the subterranean furnace, an extractor of the essences of metals.
It is described by <s>Nandi</s> for substances that are to be accomplished by blowing.
That which is twelve finger-widths deep and likewise measures a prādeśa
is furnished above, at four finger-widths, with a rim.
One should place upon the rim a disk furnished with many holes.
Putting charcoal there, one should blow through a bent tube.
This is called the gāra furnace, destructive of refined metals.
A strong tube, an aratni in measure, should be made from bottle-clay.

children.text: adhomukhaṃ ca tadvaktre nālaṃ pañcāṅgulaṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: It should face downward, and at its mouth there should be a tube five finger-widths long.
It is called the bent tube and is praised for strong blowing.
A furnace like that is prescribed for the preparation of rasa and similar substances.
It is twelve finger-widths high and four finger-widths at the bottom.
It is called the transverse-blowing furnace and purifies soft substances.
The puṭa is the indication of cooking and incineration for rasa and similar substances.
Cooking that is deficient or excessive is not desired; properly cooked medicine is beneficial.
For iron and the like, non-reversion, increase of qualities, and therefore superiority,
not sinking in water, and fullness of line-filling arise from puṭa heating.
From puṭa come color, lightness, swift pervasion, and kindling power.
Metals have greater efficacy even than fully digested chief mercury.
Just as fire standing outside enters stone through the application of puṭa,
so the acquisition of qualities such as becoming powder is certain in metals.
In a depressed square pit, two hastas across in breadth,
The medicine for heating is to be put in a puṭa filled with a thousand forest cow-dung cakes.
After enclosing it carefully in a krauñcī vessel, one should place it on top of the cake.
One should set half a thousand forest cow-dung cakes above the krauñcikā.
One should kindle the fire there; this is known as the mahāpuṭa.
A square pit, measuring by the royal cubit, should be made hollow.
Then it should be filled with a thousand cakes up to the neck and arranged.
There one should place the kumudī vessel, filled with the substance to be heated by puṭa.
As before, one should put in giriṇḍa cakes, half the amount of the cow-dung fuel.
This is called the gajapuṭa, which produces great efficacy.
In this way, when the pit is of an aratni in measure, the puṭa is called vārāha.
The puṭa on the surface of the earth which is two spans high,
and just as broad at the bottom, is the puṭa called kukkuṭaka.
The puṭa that is applied on the ground with eight forest cow-dung cakes
is called the kapotapuṭa, for making ash of young mercury.
Dry cow-dung, crushed by cows' hooves inside a cowshed and reduced to powder,
is specified as govara, the best fuel in the accomplishment of rasa.
Where a puṭa is applied with govara or else with husks,
that is called the govarapuṭa, for the successful production of rasa-ash.
In a large vessel filled with husks, with a crucible placed in the middle,
when cooking is performed by fire, that is called the vessel-puṭa.
Where, below and above, the krauñcikā is indeed covered
with heated sands, that is the sand-puṭa.
One should properly bury the fire-friendly material in the earth, two finger-widths below.
Where the puṭa is above it, that puṭa is called bhūdhara.
Where the puṭa above is made with husks or govara to the measure of sixteen parts,
that is called lāvakapuṭa, for accomplishing very soft substances.
When the measure of the puṭa has not been stated, then from the strength or weakness of the substance to be prepared,
the puṭa should be understood and applied by those skilled in reasoning by inclusion and exclusion.
Piṣṭaka, chagaṇa, chāṇa, upala, and also utpala,
giriṇḍa, upalasāṭhī, and navārī are names for cow-dung cakes.

children.text: yaḥ somadevairvihitaṃ prakīrṇamadhyāyam enaṃ prakaroti pāṭhe
children.translated_text: Whoever practices in recitation this miscellaneous chapter composed by <s>Somadeva</s>

children.text: nāsau samīheta gurūpadeśaṃ rasendravaidye'pi ca dhātuvāde ||
children.translated_text: does not need to seek instruction from a teacher even in rasendra-medicine and metallurgy.
Now the rasas are stated by <s>Somadeva</s>, those that are visibly effective,
specified in the <s>Śrīkaṇṭha Āgama</s> and excellent for accomplishing rasa.
<s>Jalotpala</s>, <s>samaṅgā</s>, <s>rasā</s>, and <s>jalapippalī</s>,
<s>Sthalaprasāriṇī</s>, <s>ciñcī</s>, <s>jālinī</s>, and <s>jalamūlakā</s>,
<s>Candrodakā</s>, <s>ardhacandrā</s>, <s>jalāpāmārga</s>, and <s>tiktakā</s>,

children.text: tuṣāmbu kākamācī ca jalakumbhī tathā śaṭī ||
children.translated_text: <s>Tuṣāmbu</s>, <s>kākamācī</s>, <s>jalakumbhī</s>, and likewise <s>śaṭī</s>,
<s>Uttamā</s>, <s>hemapuṣpī</s>, <s>durgandhā</s>, and <s>sitagandhinī</s>,

children.text: māṇḍūkī mohinī māṃsī pāṣāṇī cātha śīśikā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Māṇḍūkī</s>, <s>mohinī</s>, <s>māṃsī</s>, <s>pāṣāṇī</s>, and then <s>śīśikā</s>,
<s>Sārivā</s>, <s>lambuṣā</s>, <s>meghanādī</s>, and <s>śukanāsikā</s>,
<s>Potakī</s>, <s>hīriṇī</s>, <s>vajrakandikā</s>, and <s>aparājitā</s>,
<s>Vanamālā</s>, <s>vidārī</s>, <s>kukkuṭā</s>, and <s>halinīśvarī</s>,
<s>Vārāhī</s>, <s>bṛhatī</s>, <s>mūrvā</s>, <s>sarpākṣī</s>, and <s>sadacitrikā</s>,
<s>Mālārjuna</s>, <s>gojihvā</s>, <s>garuḍī</s>, and <s>haṃsapādikā</s>,

children.text: nandinī śikhipādī ca kāśmarī tulasī tathā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nandinī</s>, <s>śikhipādī</s>, <s>kāśmarī</s>, and likewise <s>tulasī</s>,
<s>Vanakūṣmāṇḍavallī</s>, <s>vṛścikālī</s>, and <s>veṇukā</s>,

children.text: muśalī citrapādī ca karmasphoṭī tathā viṣā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Muśalī</s>, <s>citrapādī</s>, <s>karmasphoṭī</s>, and also <s>viṣā</s>,
<s>Ajamārī</s>, <s>pāṭalā</s>, <s>paṭolī</s>, and <s>dhanvayāsaka</s>,

children.text: bhārṅgī viṣaghnī guḍūcī vāsā bhṛṅgī ca pāgavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Bhārṅgī</s>, <s>viṣaghnī</s>, <s>guḍūcī</s>, <s>vāsā</s>, <s>bhṛṅgī</s>, and <s>pāgava</s>:
thus sixty-eight powerful rasa-medicinal herbs are stated.
They are used in binding and māraṇa, and likewise in jāraṇa and regulation,
in binding and taking up mercury, and in the removal of all its faults.

children.text: vindhyādrau himaparvate ca malaye gomantake śrīgirau sahyādrāvatha pāriyātrakagirau kiṣkindhanāmālaye
children.translated_text: On <s>Vindhya</s>, on the <s>Himalaya</s>, on <s>Malaya</s>, on <s>Gomantaka</s>, on <s>Śrīgiri</s>, on <s>Sahyādri</s>, and on <s>Pāriyātra</s>, and in the range named <s>Kiṣkindhā</s>,

children.text: māhendre'pyatha mālyavatkṣitidhare tadrūpanāmādhikaṃ gopābhīrakasiddhavaidyamukhato vaidyaiḥ samāvedyatām ||
children.translated_text: and also on <s>Mahendra</s> and on the mountain <s>Mālyavat</s>, physicians should learn their forms and additional local names from the mouths of cowherds, Ābhīras, siddhas, and physicians.
<s>Sarpākṣī</s>, <s>vandhyakarkoṭī</s>, <s>jalabimbī</s>, and <s>jambukī</s>,
<s>Punarnavā</s>, <s>matsyākṣī</s>, <s>bhṛṅgarāja</s>, and <s>śatāvarī</s>,
<s>Śarapuṅkhā</s>, <s>maṇḍūkaparṇikā</s>, and <s>brahmadaṇḍikā</s>,
<s>Anantā</s>, <s>kukkuṭī</s>, <s>jaṅghā</s>, <s>kākamācī</s>, and <s>śikhaṇḍinī</s>,
<s>Sahadevī</s>, <s>kapotī</s>, <s>viṣṇukrāntā</s>, and <s>kuraṇṭaka</s>,
<s>Mahābalā</s>, <s>nāgabalā</s>, <s>mūrvā</s>, <s>rāsnā</s>, and <s>kuriṅginī</s>,
<s>Phaṇi</s>, <s>nīlī</s>, <s>prapunnāṭa</s>, and <s>samaṅgāmalakī</s>,
<s>Jvālinī</s>, <s>meghanāda</s>, <s>gojihvā</s>, and <s>padmacāriṇī</s>,
<s>Pāṭhā</s>, <s>kokilākṣa</s>, <s>tripattrā</s>, and <s>ākhukarṇikā</s>,

children.text: ekaparṇī dviparṇī ca triparṇī kṣīriṇī tathā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Ekaparṇī</s>, <s>dviparṇī</s>, <s>triparṇī</s>, and likewise <s>kṣīriṇī</s>,
<s>Tittiḍī</s>, <s>meṣaśṛṅgī</s>, <s>tulasī</s>, and <s>śyāmaparṇikā</s>,
and <s>śvetādriparṇikā</s>: this is held to be the group beginning with <s>sarpākṣī</s>.
Known as the set of forty-six, it regulates mercury.
Here the five parts of the herbs should be collected according to rule.
In the sweating of rasas and the like, in bringing into the crucible, and in purification,
eight or more should be taken, according to availability, for the operations that have been stated.
An increase beyond groups of eight certainly produces an increase of qualities.
<s>Vyāghrikā</s>, <s>rākṣasī</s>, <s>vahni</s>, <s>cāṇḍālī</s>, and <s>gajakarṇikā</s>,
<s>Ṣaṭkārī</s>, <s>śaṅkhapuṣpī</s>, <s>bṛhatī</s>, and <s>hilamocaka</s>,
<s>Śṛgālajihvikā</s>, <s>vahni</s>, <s>madanī</s>, and likewise <s>lāṅgalī</s>,
<s>Cakrikā</s>, <s>vajriṇī</s>, <s>vyāghrī</s>, <s>kaṅkatī</s>, and <s>putrajīvikā</s>.
<s>Kañcukī</s> and likewise <s>Karkoṭī</s>, <s>Kumārī</s>, and <s>Padmacāriṇī</s>;

children.text: ekavīrā rudantī ca lakṣmī narakasā tathā
children.translated_text: <s>Ekavīrā</s>, <s>Rudantī</s>, and <s>Lakṣmī</s>, and also <s>Narakasā</s>;
<s>Uccaṭā</s>, <s>Raktacitrā</s>, <s>Nāginī</s>, and <s>Nāgavallikā</s>;
<s>Saktukā</s>, <s>Saktuśṛṅgī</s>, <s>Raktasnuh</s>, and <s>Yajñavallikā</s>;
<s>Śākhoṭa</s>, <s>Meṣaśṛṅgī</s>, <s>Hemalī</s>, and <s>Vyāghrapādikā</s>;
<s>Śamī</s>, <s>Vyāghranakhī</s>, <s>Somavallarī</s>, and <s>Arkapuṣpikā</s>;
<s>Keśinī</s>, <s>Kāsamārī</s>, <s>Vṛkṣarāja</s>, and <s>Ajamārikā</s>;
<s>Koṭarākṣī</s>, <s>Hanūmantī</s>, <s>Narajīvā</s>, and <s>Aṅganāyakī</s>;

children.text: mālikā kākatuṇḍī ca meghapuṣpī ca kaṅguṇī ||
children.translated_text: <s>Mālikā</s>, <s>Kākatuṇḍī</s>, <s>Meghapuṣpī</s>, and <s>Kaṅguṇī</s>;
And another, <s>Tuvaravallī</s>, together with <s>Jagatī</s> and <s>Haṃsapādikā</s>;

children.text: kumbhinī vahnimārī ca sūryabhaktā ca vākucī ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kumbhinī</s>, <s>Vahnimārī</s>, <s>Sūryabhaktā</s>, and <s>Vākucī</s>;
<s>Rasanirjīvakārī</s>, <s>Bhūśuṇḍī</s>, and <s>Kaṭutumbikā</s>;
<s>Devadālī</s>, <s>Viśālā</s>, <s>Kārpāsī</s>, and <s>Brahmarañjaka</s>;
Likewise <s>Kṛṣṇākṣīva</s>, <s>Kṛṣṇadhattūra</s>, and <s>Vanapīluka</s>;

children.text: śvetārko yavaciñcā ca kāravellī ca dantikā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Śvetārka</s>, <s>Yavaciñcā</s>, <s>Kāravellī</s>, and <s>Dantikā</s>;

children.text: gojihvā kākajaṅghā ca śvetaguñjā ca śambarā
children.translated_text: <s>Gojihvā</s>, <s>Kākajaṅghā</s>, <s>Śvetaguñjā</s>, and <s>Śambarā</s>;
<s>Mahākālī</s>, <s>Sitāṅkola</s>, <s>Māyūra</s>, and <s>Paṭolikā</s>:
this group beginning with <s>Vyāghrikā</s> is the supreme maker of mercury-ash.
In the seeds of the herbs stated here, <s>pārada</s> (mercury) is digested one by one.
<s>Raktasnuhī</s>, <s>Rudantī</s>, <s>Raktāgni</s>, and <s>Somavallikā</s>;
<s>Vṛddhadāru</s>, <s>Śākhoṭī</s>, <s>Mohinī</s>, and <s>Aṅgāravallikā</s>;
<s>Barhikā</s>, <s>Kṣīramārjārī</s>, <s>Triśūlā</s>, and <s>Kṣīrakukkuṭī</s>;
<s>Jīmūta</s>, <s>Kākamācī</s>, <s>Nīlikā</s>, and <s>Śaṅkhapuṣpikā</s>;
having leaves shaped like leaves of <s>Nāgavallī</s>, and having a small bulb;

children.text: śrīśailotthā ca vajraghnī nāgakarṇīti sā smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: born on <s>Śrīśaila</s>, destroyer of diamond, it is remembered as <s>Nāgakarṇī</s>.
<s>Jyotiṣmatī</s>, <s>Drumajyotis</s>, <s>Tṛṇajyotis</s>, and then <s>Uccaṭā</s>;
<s>Udumbarī</s>, <s>Tridaṇḍī</s>, and another, <s>Nīlajyotis</s>;
<s>Hemavallarikā</s>, <s>Tāmravallarī</s>, and <s>Cukra</s> as well;
<s>Tridaṇḍī</s>, <s>Brahmadaṇḍī</s>, <s>Krauñcikā</s>, and <s>Sthalapadminī</s>;

children.text: varā vartulaparṇā ca nāgakaṇṭhī ca lāṅgalī
children.translated_text: <s>Varā</s>, <s>Vartulaparṇā</s>, <s>Nāgakaṇṭhī</s>, and <s>Lāṅgalī</s>;
<s>Nāgajihvā</s>, <s>Arkapatrī</s>, and likewise <s>Kāṣṭhodumbarikā</s>;
<s>Kāladaṇḍī</s> and <s>Triparṇī</s>: this is the group beginning with <s>Raktasnuhī</s>.

children.text: rasabandhe vadhe śuddhau vihitaḥ śambhunā svayam ||
children.translated_text: It was prescribed by <s>Śambhu</s> himself for the binding, killing, and purification of <s>rasa</s> (mercury).
With vegetable substances endowed with tactile quality, smell, and taste,

children.text: śodhito marditaḥ sūto mriyate badhyate sukham ||
children.translated_text: <s>sūta</s> (mercury), purified and triturated, is killed and bound with ease.
<s>Kadalī</s>, <s>Sūryabhakta</s>, and likewise <s>Kaṭukoṣātakī</s>;
<s>Drāviṇī</s>, <s>Kākamācī</s>, <s>Śigrukā</s>, and <s>Kṣīrakañcukī</s>;
and <s>Nīrapippalikā</s>: this is the group beginning with <s>Kadalī</s>.
It is certainly the liquefier of all metals and also of substances beginning with <s>rasa</s>.
<s>Kākamācī</s>, <s>Arkapatrī</s>, <s>Kāsamarda</s>, and <s>Kṛtāñjali</s>;
<s>Lakṣmaṇā</s>, <s>Haṃsapādī</s>, <s>Nāginī</s>, and <s>Kṣīranālikā</s>;
<s>Tāmbūlī</s>, <s>Vyālikā</s>, <s>Brāhmī</s>, <s>Kāravellī</s>, <s>Arjunī</s>, and <s>Carā</s>;
<s>Vārāhakarṇikā</s>, <s>Meghadhvani</s>, and <s>Sahadevikā</s>;
and likewise <s>Kuruvaka</s>: this is the group beginning with <s>Kākamācī</s>.

children.text: krāmaṇāya vinirdiṣṭā dehe lohe rasasya hi ||
children.translated_text: It is prescribed for the penetration of <s>rasa</s> into the body and into metal.
<s>Ekavīrā</s>, <s>Mahāvīrā</s>, <s>Prayoga</s>, and <s>Hemadaṇḍikā</s>:
this fourfold set is taught as certain in the binding of <s>rasa</s>.
All of it acts on body and metal and removes great diseases.
It is blessed, gives sons, and is aphrodisiac through sight, touch, and the like.
A creeper with leaves like those of a corpse, bearing a single fruit at its fall,
is called <s>Ekavīrā</s>; it is the supreme agent for binding <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: ekamekaṃ phalaṃ yasyāḥ pare patre prajāyate
children.translated_text: That on which a single fruit is produced on each separate leaf,
with a color like coral, is considered <s>Mahāvīrā</s>.
Having three bulbs and three shoots, and two fruits attached to the stalk,
with leaves resembling bamboo leaves, born on <s>Gajavindhyācala</s>,

children.text: tasya madhyamakando hi prayogo nāma rākṣasaḥ
children.translated_text: its middle bulb is the rākṣasa named <s>Prayoga</s>.

children.text: tena saṃmarditaḥ sūto mriyate badhyate sukham ||
children.translated_text: Triturated with it, <s>sūta</s> (mercury) is killed and bound with ease.
Having leaves like betel leaves, golden-colored, and milky,
and lacking fruit, flowers, and the like, it is considered <s>Hemavallī</s>.
When it has been used in conjunction, the <s>pārada</s> bound with that urine,
held in the mouth for a year, grants the power of moving through the sky.
<s>Vajradaṇḍa</s>, <s>Laśunadaṇḍa</s>, and <s>Lohadaṇḍa</s>: these three
have the nature of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, and <s>Śiva</s>, and protect the three worlds.

children.text: pathyā śuṇṭhī śilā muṇḍī nirguṇḍī ca viḍaṅgakam
children.translated_text: <s>Pathyā</s>, <s>Śuṇṭhī</s>, <s>Śilā</s>, <s>Muṇḍī</s>, <s>Nirguṇḍī</s>, and <s>Viḍaṅgaka</s>;
<s>Citraka</s>, <s>Trikaṭu</s>, <s>Hemamākṣika</s>, and likewise <s>Vimala</s>;
this class beginning with <s>Vajradaṇḍa</s> is exceedingly excellent in rasāyana.
It is the best remover of all diseases and destroyer of old age and death.
<s>Bhūpāṭalī</s>, <s>Paṭolī</s>, <s>Yogārī</s>, and <s>Siṃhavallikā</s>;

children.text: śūkarī hemavallī ca nāgadhārī ca mārkavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Śūkarī</s>, <s>Hemavallī</s>, <s>Nāgadhārī</s>, and <s>Mārkava</s>;
this class beginning with <s>Bhūpāṭalī</s> brings about the binding of <s>rasa</s>.
<s>Pāṭalendīvarī</s> and also <s>Mantrasiṃhāsanī</s>;
<s>Niśācarī</s>, <s>Kaṅkālakhecarī</s>, and <s>Pañcaratnaka</s>;
it acts on body and metal, and brings about the killing and binding of <s>sūta</s>.
It destroys wrinkles and grey hair and is the supreme remover of all diseases.

children.text: ghṛtaṃ khaṇḍo mākṣikaṃ ca vijñeyaṃ madhuratrayam
children.translated_text: Ghee, sugar, and honey should be known as the sweet triad.
The urines of elephant, camel, buffalo, donkey, and horse,

children.text: go'jāvīnāṃ striyaḥ puṃsāṃ puṣpaṃ bījaṃ ca yojayet
children.translated_text: of cows, goats, and sheep, both female and male; one should add menstrual fluid and seed.
Brick, red ocher, salt, ash, and anthill clay
are called the five earths by those skilled in the application of <s>rasa</s>.
<s>Ṭaṅkaṇa</s>, <s>Yavakṣāra</s>, and <s>Sarjikṣāra</s> as the third;
There are <s>palāśa</s>, banana, <s>śigru</s>, sesame, <s>apāmārga</s>, and <s>mokṣaka</s>,
radish, tamarind, <s>bodhi</s>, red <s>rājagiri</s>, and so forth.
There are also <s>kambala</s> and <s>aparakuḍya</s>; the alkalis from these are of various kinds.
This is called the alkaline group; it stimulates digestion and has great force.
It performs the <s>jāraṇa</s> (digestion or calcination) of gems and the like, and also of all metals and similar substances.
Sour <s>vetasa</s>, <s>jambīra</s>, <s>nimbuka</s>, and <s>rājanimbuka</s>,

children.text: badaraṃ bījapūraṃ ca tintiḍī cukrikā tathā
children.translated_text: <s>badara</s>, <s>bījapūra</s>, tamarind, and <s>cukrikā</s>,
<s>caṇāmla</s>, <s>kāñjika</s> in the same way, <s>amlikā</s>, and sour pomegranate,
<s>karamarda</s> and sour jujube: this is called the acid group.
It is useful for the purification of mercury and the rest, and for liquefaction and <s>jāraṇa</s>.
Sea salt, salt produced from the <s>Sindhu</s>, glass-derived salt, and that called <s>viḍa</s>,

children.text: sauvarcalamatho raumaṃ cullikaṃ ca gaḍādi ca ||
children.translated_text: <s>sauvarcala</s>, then <s>rauma</s>, <s>cullika</s>, <s>gaḍa</s>, and so on:
this is the group of salts; it gives relish, digests, and kindles digestion.
It liquefies and purifies all metals and also ashes.

children.text: śṛṅgikaṃ kālakūṭaṃ ca vatsanābhaṃ ca saktukam
children.translated_text: <s>śṛṅgika</s>, <s>kālakūṭa</s>, <s>vatsanābha</s>, and <s>saktuka</s>,

children.text: pītaṃ ca viṣavargo'yaṃ sa varaḥ parikīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the yellow poison: this poison group is proclaimed the excellent one.
It is recommended in mercury work, and also for its binding and killing.
But if it is taken without proper method, it certainly kills.

children.text: lāṅgalī viṣamuṣṭiśca karavīraś ca jayā tathā
children.translated_text: <s>lāṅgalī</s>, <s>viṣamuṣṭi</s>, <s>karavīra</s>, and <s>jayā</s>,
<s>nīlaka</s>, <s>kanaka</s>, and <s>arka</s>: this is the group consisting of subsidiary poisons.

children.text: dīpanaḥ pācano bhedī rase kvāpi ca yujyate
children.translated_text: It stimulates digestion, digests, and breaks open the bowels; it is sometimes used in mercury.
Among mobile poisons and the like, there is no poison superior to that of the snake.
The oils of sesame, linseed, safflower, neem, and <s>karaja</s>,
and also of <s>rājī</s>, <s>siddhārthaka</s>, and the seeds of <s>guñjā</s> and <s>kaṅguṇī</s>,

children.text: madhūkasya ca tailaiśca tailavargo rase hitaḥ
children.translated_text: and the oils of <s>madhūka</s>: this oil group is useful in mercury work.
Elephant, horse, woman, cow, she-ass, she-goat, and ewe,
she-camel, <s>udumbara</s>, <s>aśvattha</s>, <s>bhānu</s>, <s>nyagrodha</s>, and <s>tilvaka</s>,
<s>dugdhikā</s>, the <s>snuh</s> group, and likewise <s>uttamakarṇikā</s>:
the milks or latexes of these are prescribed as the milk group in mercury and related operations.
With the biles of buffalo, boar, fish, goat, and peacock,
of black snake, <s>rohita</s> fish, and cat,
the bile group is taught for killing, binding, and impregnating mercury.
With fat produced from the flesh of frog, tortoise, boar, snake, and man,
the fat group too is praised in mercury work.
Of the <s>pārāvata</s>, the <s>cāṣa</s> bird, the dove, and the peacock,
and of the vulture and also the cock, the excrement group is indeed specified.
It purifies all metals through heating in a <s>puṭa</s> and through smearing.
Safflower, <s>khadira</s>, lac, madder, and red sandalwood,

children.text: adrī ca bandhujīvaṃ ca tathā karpūragandhinī
children.translated_text: <s>adrī</s>, <s>bandhujīva</s>, and likewise <s>karpūragandhinī</s>,
and <s>mākṣika</s>: this should be known as the red group, a very strong colorant.
<s>kiṃśuka</s>, <s>karṇikāra</s>, and the two kinds of turmeric:
this yellow group is prescribed in the work of the king of mercury.

children.text: tagaraḥ kuṭajaṃ kundo guñjā jīvantikā tathā
children.translated_text: <s>tagara</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, jasmine, <s>guñjā</s>, and <s>jīvantikā</s>,
and the white lotus root: this is declared to be the white group.

children.text: kadalī krūravallī ca triphalā nīlikā nalaḥ
children.translated_text: Banana, <s>krūravallī</s>, <s>triphala</s>, <s>nīlikā</s>, reed,
mud, green vitriol, and unripe mango: this is declared to be the black group.
By means of the red group and the other groups, any substance that has the nature of <s>jāraṇa</s>
should be carefully impregnated, so as to obtain the corresponding color.
The group is held to be purifiable by glass, borax, and <s>śiprā</s>.
It destroys the impurities of essences, of bound mercury, and of metals,
and is said by mercury-workers to destroy the <s>kāpālika</s> group.
Here buffalo horn and ram horn, joined with seeds produced in <s>Kaliṅga</s>,
and hare bones: this formula destroys the hardness of metals.
With jaggery, guggulu, <s>guñjā</s>, ghee, <s>sāragha</s>, and borax,
this group is held to liquefy all metals and the like that are difficult to melt.
All alkalis destroy impurity; acids are for purification and <s>jāraṇa</s>.

children.text: māndyaṃ viṣāṇi nighnanti snaigdhyaṃ snehāḥ prakurvate ||
children.translated_text: Poisons destroy sluggishness; oils produce unctuousness.
The great minerals are mica, <s>rājāvarta</s>, <s>vaikrānta</s>, <s>sasyaka</s>, <s>vimala</s>, and mountain-born mineral,

children.text: tutthaṃ ca tāpyaṃ ca rasāyanāste sattvāni teṣām amṛtopamāni ||
children.translated_text: together with blue vitriol and pyrite; they are elixirs, and their essences are like nectar.

children.text: gaurītejaḥ paramam amṛtaṃ vātapittakṣayaghnaṃ prajñodbodhi praśamitarujaṃ vṛṣyam āyuṣyam agryam
children.translated_text: <s>Gaurītejas</s> is the supreme nectar: it destroys wind, bile, and wasting, awakens intelligence, calms pain, is aphrodisiac, life-giving, and foremost.

children.text: balyaṃ snigdhaṃ rucidam akaphaṃ dīpanaṃ śītavīryaṃ tattadyogaiḥ sakalagadahṛd vyoma sūtendrabandhi ||
children.translated_text: It is strengthening, unctuous, relish-giving, non-phlegmatic, digestive, and cold in potency; with its various preparations, mica removes every disease and binds the lord mercury.
Mica brought from a mine below the measure of a royal hand
will give the stated result; if it lacks essence, it is utterly fruitless.
<s>Pināka</s>, <s>nāga</s>, <s>maṇḍūka</s>, and <s>vajra</s> are regarded as kinds of mica.
According to the distinction of white and other colors, each of these is fourfold.
<s>Pināka</s>-mica, heated strongly by fire, releases a mass of flakes.
When consumed, it binds the feces and certainly kills a human being.
<s>Nāga</s>-mica, placed in fire, makes a sound like lead.

children.text: tadbhuktaṃ kurute kuṣṭhaṃ maṇḍalākhyaṃ na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When eaten, it causes the skin disease called <s>maṇḍala</s>, without doubt.
Mica that, when blown in the furnace, leaps up again and again and falls is <s>maṇḍūka</s>.
It causes stone disease, incurable except by surgery.
<s>Vajra</s>-mica, heated by fire, is free from every defect,
and that produces benefit for the body and metals; it is supreme and removes all diseases.

children.text: śvetaṃ raktaṃ ca pītaṃ ca kṛṣṇamevaṃ caturvidham
children.translated_text: White, red, yellow, and black: in this way it is fourfold.
White is praised for white operations, while red and the others are used in yellow operations.
Although the excellent <s>vyoma</s> (mica) has been described as fourfold in <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenative alchemy),
nevertheless the kind resembling a black color is many millions of times superior.
It should be unctuous, with broad layers, resistant to fire, and especially heavy;
and its sheets should be easy to separate. That <s>abhraka</s> (mica) is declared praiseworthy.
Mica that still has <s>candra</s> (glitter), resembling glass dross, should not be made to feed <s>rasa</s> (mercury).
If <s>rasa</s> has consumed it, that mercury is not to be used either with metals or in <s>rasāyana</s>.

children.text: niścandrikaṃ mṛtaṃ vyoma sevyaṃ sarvagadeṣu ca
children.translated_text: Dead mica, free from glitter, is to be used in all diseases;
but when taken while still glittering, it brings on urinary disease and weak digestion.
Those without proper method who have taught a <s>rasāyana</s> made from leaf-mica
have prescribed the poison called <s>Kālakūṭa</s> as a means to life.
For the sake of extracting <s>sattva</s> and for internal use, purified <s>abhraka</s> should be employed;
otherwise, by producing bad qualities, it certainly causes disorder.
Mica heated red-hot seven times and cast into sour gruel

children.text: nirdoṣaṃ jāyate nūnaṃ nikṣiptaṃ vāpi gojale ||
children.translated_text: surely becomes free from defects; or it may be cast into cow's liquid.
It may also be cast into a decoction of <s>Triphala</s>, or especially into cow's milk.
Then, after making <s>dhānyābhraka</s> (grain-processed mica), one should grind it with the juices of <s>Matsyākṣikā</s>.
Having made discs and then dried them, one should cook them in a half-elephant <s>puṭa</s> furnace-charge;
in this way it should indeed be cooked six times together with the juices of <s>Paunarnava</s>.
One may also triturate the mica with <s>ṭaṅkaṇa</s> (borax) in due proportion and make it into discs;
then likewise it should certainly be cooked seven times with half-elephant <s>puṭa</s>s.
In the same way, with the juice of <s>Vāsā</s> and with the juice of <s>Taṇḍulīya</s>,
one should give it seven further cookings according to the previously stated procedure.
The <s>ghana</s> (processed mica) perfected in this way should be used in all formulations,
mixed with one-quarter part <s>ṭaṅkaṇa</s> and triturated with <s>Matsyākṣī</s> juice.

children.text: rundhyāt koṣṭhyāṃ dṛḍhaṃ dhmātaṃ sattvarūpaṃ bhaved ghanam
children.translated_text: Sealed firmly in a furnace and blown, the <s>ghana</s> becomes of the nature of <s>sattva</s>.
Then, having made it into fine cloth-sifted powder and drenched it with cow ghee,
